full_judgment:
6. It is, therefore, clear that the prayer for review was made by the Government on the same ground on which its tenant had lost previously. Be that as it may, the review petitions have been rejected mainly on the ground of limitation and not on merit. 

 7. The review petitions were filed after 580 days of the passing of the judgment in the writ petitions without filing any application under section 5 of the Limitation Act. Government gave explanation of the long delay in the review petitions which was considered by the High Court Division but was not accepted. 

 9. We have perused the impugned judgment and considered the circumstances as set out in the review petitions under which the said petitions were filed after such a long delay. We have particularly perused paragraph 16 of the review petition in which the relevant facts since the passing of the judgment in the writ petitions have been set out. There is no mention as to when the Government became aware for the first time about the sale deeds of 1967 on the basis of which review was prayed for. It appears further that the Ministry of Works by its Memo dated 16.3.1993 requested the office of the solicitor to prefer an appeal against the judgment passed in the writ petition. The solicitor and the Ministry of Law took the view that instead of an appeal a review petition should be filed and accordingly the solicitor's office forwarded the relevant file to the Deputy Attorney-General (writ) on 19.10.1993. Thereafter certified copies of the sale deeds were obtained through the solicitor's office and were received in the office of the Deputy Attorney General (writ) on 27.2.1994. The review applications were filed on 3.4.1994. The learned Additional Attorney-General submits that since the review applications were filed within less than 2 months of the receipt of the certified copies of the sale deeds, the High Court Division should have condoned the delay. The argument is not convincing because there is no statement as to when the Government became aware of the sale deeds for the first time and decided to take a review. It is however, clear that the Government came with the review petitions after its tenant had failed in his attempt to get an order of review. It is on record that the Government was also made a party in the previous review applications filed by the tenant. The learned Additional Attorney-General does not dispute that the limitation for a review petition was only 20 days. 

 11. As already noticed the review petitions have been dismissed mainly on the ground of limitation and it cannot be said that the impugned judgment is wholly unreasonable on that point or that the matter has not been properly dealt with. Since the passing of the judgment in the writ petitions there has been a long delay and the belated review applications could not be accepted on the alleged ground of discovery of new facts without clearly disclosing as to when the new facts came to light.
